title: Homework 2
text:
For this first task, we created vectors for pre-treatment and post-treatment from a medical experiment on blood pressure. We assigned a name to these vectors, and then calculate difference between the respective vectors to determine average difference.

Create two vectors. One vector corresponding to the pre measurements and one to the post measurements.

# Creating Initial Vectors
pre_tr <- c(130, 128, 116, 124, 133, 134, 118, 126, 114, 127, 141, 138, 128, 140, 137, 131, 120, 128, 139, 135)

post_tr <- c(114, 98, 113, 99, 107, 116, 113, 111, 119, 117, 101, 119, 130, 122, 106, 106, 124, 102, 117, 113)

Assign names to the vector elements using the paste() function. Note that names() can be overwritten by a character vector. To quickly create the names, try running the code. Create the same names for each vector’s elements.

# Vector and patients IDs
subject_ids <- paste("Subject", 1:20, sep = "_")

names(pre_tr) <- subject_ids
names(post_tr) <- subject_ids

Calculate the change in blood pressure for each patient by subtracting post-treatment measurements from pre-treatment measurements. Recall that R does math element-wise! Save this calculation as a new object (also a vector).

# The change in blood pressure across all patients
diff_bp <- pre_tr - post_tr
diff_bp

        16         30          3         25         26         18          5 
 Subject_8  Subject_9 Subject_10 Subject_11 Subject_12 Subject_13 Subject_14 
        15         -5         10         40         19         -2         18 
Subject_15 Subject_16 Subject_17 Subject_18 Subject_19 Subject_20 
        31         25         -4         26         22         22 


Calculate the average decrease in blood pressure across all patients.

# Calculating the average in blood pressure across all patients
avg_diff <- mean(diff_bp)
avg_diff

[1] 17


The average of all 20 patients the blood pressure dropped by 17 points.
Determine which patients experienced a decrease in blood pressure after treatment (a positive change). Use the which() function to just return the indices (and names) associated with this type of change.

# Find subjects with a positive blood pressure change
decreased_bp <- which(diff_bp > 0) # which() returns positions, but not the actual                                              #difference themselves.
decreased_bp

         1          2          3          4          5          6          7 
 Subject_8 Subject_10 Subject_11 Subject_12 Subject_14 Subject_15 Subject_16 
         8         10         11         12         14         15         16 
Subject_18 Subject_19 Subject_20 
        18         19         20 


Based on the output, we can see how subjects 9,13, and 17 are not part of the list, indicating that their blood pressure went up after the treatment. Thus, the treatment didn’t help them.
Subset the vector of differences to only return those that have a positive change.

# Return only positive blood pressure changes

# Method 1: filter directly on the logical condition
positive_diff <- diff_bp[diff_bp > 0]
positive_diff

 Subject_1  Subject_2  Subject_3  Subject_4  Subject_5  Subject_6  Subject_7 
        16         30          3         25         26         18          5 
 Subject_8 Subject_10 Subject_11 Subject_12 Subject_14 Subject_15 Subject_16 
        15         10         40         19         18         31         25 
Subject_18 Subject_19 Subject_20 
        26         22         22 

# Method 2: reuses the indices from the previous which() used in step 5. 
# this method more efficient since decreased_bp is already computed.
positive_diff <- diff_bp[decreased_bp]
positive_diff

 Subject_1  Subject_2  Subject_3  Subject_4  Subject_5  Subject_6  Subject_7 
        16         30          3         25         26         18          5 
 Subject_8 Subject_10 Subject_11 Subject_12 Subject_14 Subject_15 Subject_16 
        15         10         40         19         18         31         25 
Subject_18 Subject_19 Subject_20 
        26         22         22 

# Both methods return the same result. Method 1 was chosen for the final approach as it reads clearly without having to go back to step 5.

In this case we know that subjects 9, 13 and 17 are the patients whose blood pressure went up after the treatment.
Calculate the average decrease in blood pressure for those where the blood pressure decreased (positive change).

# Average decrease in blood pressure for positive change valus 
avg_diff_decreased <- mean(positive_diff)
avg_diff_decreased

[1] 20.64706


Comparing the two resulted averages, notice how when we included everyone, the average decreased by 17, however this resulted included 3 patients whose blood pressure did not decrease. After we calculated the average only including the 17 patients who blood pressure improved, the average decreases about 20.65 points. This results is more accurate to identify the effectiveness of the treatment.

Task 4: Control Flow Practice

Suppose we want to characterize the post-treatment (or placebo) blood pressure measurement as optimal (≤ 120), borderline (120 < bp ≤ 130), and high (> 130). First, create a new column in each data frame from above called status. You can do this via
your_df$status <- character(20) #or 10 depending on number of observations
Note: You want to add this additional column to the data frames that are stored in your list (R doesn’t do referencing to the original object).

experiment_list$treatment$status <- character(nrow(experiment_list$treatment))
experiment_list$placebo$status <- character(nrow(experiment_list$placebo))

For the non-placebo data frame (within the list), create a for loop and use if/then/else logic to create the status column’s values.

for (i in 1:nrow(experiment_list$treatment)) {
  bp_value <- experiment_list$treatment$post_bp[i]
  if (bp_value <= 120) {
    experiment_list$treatment$status[i] <- "optimal"
  } else if (bp_value > 120 & bp_value <= 130) {
    experiment_list$treatment$status[i] <- "borderline"
  } else {
    experiment_list$treatment$status[i] <- "high"
  }
}

R projects is an easy way to divide and organize your work. Each project contains a working directory, its own workspace, history, as well as folder structure & source documents.

What is Git and what is GitHub?

Git is a version control software, used so that we can periodically save snapshots of our files/work, whereas GitHub is the online platform that stores our git repositories.
GitHub is also key for collaboration with others, so that multiple people can share snapshots of repos and work on them at the same time and push it to the platform.

What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?

Tibble is similar to a data.frame, but it is a modern re-imagining that’s more compatible for the wonderful tidyverse library.
They have a more compact print, and complain more upfront leading to cleaner code.
Subsetting one column using [ preserves the tibble, but df forces it down to a vector.

Task 4: Control Flow Practice

Suppose we want to characterize the post-treatment (or placebo) blood pressure measurement as optimal (≤ 120), borderline (120 < bp ≤ 130), and high (> 130). First, create a new column in each data frame from above called status. You can do this via

for (i in 1:nrow(experiment_list$treatment)) {

  if (bp_value <= 120) {
    experiment_list$treatment$status[i] <- "optimal"
  } else if (bp_value > 120 & bp_value <= 130) {
    experiment_list$treatment$status[i] <- "borderline"
  } else {
    experiment_list$treatment$status[i] <- "high"

Task 4: Writing Functions

Interquartile Range Function
First, I create a function called getIQR that calculates the interquartile range by subtracting the 25th percentile from the 75th percentile. The returned value is unnamed, and additional arguments can be passed to quantile().

getIQR <- function(x, ...) {
  result <- quantile(x, 0.75, ...) - quantile(x, 0.25, ...)
  unname(result)
}

I apply the function to the fixed_acidity and citric_acid columns of the combined wine data.

getIQR(wine_data$fixed_acidity)

[1] 1.3

getIQR(wine_data$citric_acid)

[1] 0.14




Coefficient of Variation Function
Next, I create a function called getCoefVar that calculates the sample coefficient of variation as the sample standard deviation divided by the absolute value of the sample mean.

getCoefVar <- function(x, ...) {
  sd(x, ...) / abs(mean(x, ...))
}

I apply this function to the same two variables.

getCoefVar(wine_data$fixed_acidity)

[1] 0.1796783

getCoefVar(wine_data$citric_acid)

[1] 0.4560663




Summary Function
Next, I create a wrapper function called getSummaries. This function calls the two functions created above and returns both the IQR and coefficient of variation with appropriate names.

getSummaries <- function(x, ...) {
  c(
    IQR = getIQR(x, ...),
    CoefVar = getCoefVar(x, ...)
  )

Write a basic function (call it getIQR) that takes in a vector of numbers and returns the interquartile range (75th percentile - 25th percentile). You can use the quantile function. Remove the name on the returned vector (i.e. make sure the returned item doesn’t have a name like 75% or something like that). Allow your function to pass unnamed arguments to the quantile function.

getIQR <- function(x, ...) {
  q <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), ...)
  unname(q[2] - q[1])
}
